summary: Describes extensions to TN3270, the protocol for using IBM 3270 terminals over a network, to select a specific LU name and printer. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some old mainframe screens can be reached through a network. This adds a way to pick which screen or printer to use.

questions: how to select specific lu in tn3270
subtitle: Extensions to select specific IBM 3270 terminals and manage printing.

tldr.problem: IBM mainframe applications rely on specific terminal (LU) and printer assignments, controlled through VTAM configuration. Users accessing 3270 terminals over TCP/IP had no way to request a particular terminal or manage printer status.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1646 defines two extensions to TN3270: a way to request a specific Logical Unit (LU) name in the TERMINAL-TYPE negotiation, and a protocol for 3270 printers (TN3287) to report status back to the host application.
tldr.outcome: These extensions allowed TCP/IP networks to connect IBM 3270 terminals and printers while maintaining compatibility with existing VTAM/SNA application infrastructure.

today: RFC 1646 provided a practical way to connect IBM 3270 terminals and printers over TCP/IP networks. While mainframe use has declined, legacy systems continue to run these protocols in many enterprises. The TN3270 standard evolved with later RFCs (such as RFC 2355, TN3270 Extensions), but RFC 1646's printer extensions remain foundational. Modern terminal emulators still implement this protocol to support existing mainframe applications.

sections.title: Connecting Mainframes to TCP/IP Networks
sections.content:
IBM mainframes have been serving thousands of users daily for decades through 3270 terminals. Many organizations wanted to add TCP/IP network support without rewriting these mainframe applications. TN3270, the TELNET protocol for 3270 terminals, provided a bridge, but early versions lacked features needed for full compatibility.

RFC 1646 addresses a critical gap: IBM mainframe applications use Logical Unit (LU) names to identify specific terminals and printers within the VTAM/SNA hierarchy. When a TN3270 client connects, there was no standard way to specify which LU it wanted. Additionally, IBM 3270 printers communicate status information back to the mainframe (whether they are ready, out of paper, or disconnected), and TN3270 lacked a protocol for this out-of-band communication.
sections.eli5: Mainframe applications know specific terminals by name. An old system would say "connect to terminal LU5". This RFC adds the ability to ask for a specific terminal by name when connecting through the network.

sections.title: VTAM/SNA Concepts in TN3270
sections.content:
The RFC explains key VTAM/SNA concepts needed to understand the solution. A Physical Unit (PU) represents a terminal controller, and Logical Units (LUs) represent individual terminals attached to it. The SSCP-LU session carries out-of-band management information, while the LU-LU session carries application data. VTAM tables called LOGMODE tables define session parameters: whether to use brackets and chaining, the terminal type (LU 1 for printers, LU 2 for screens, LU 3 for printer-screens), and the screen size.

When a session starts, a BIND message exchanges these settings, and they cannot be changed during the session. LU 1 and LU 3 printers can coexist on the same host, often due to printer sharing between applications like CICS and JES. The solution must handle mixing both types.
sections.eli5: Mainframe terminals are organized in a hierarchy: controllers contain individual terminals. Each terminal is told at connection time what protocol to use and what size its screen is. These settings cannot change once the session starts.

sections.title: TN3287 Printer Protocol and Terminal Selection
sections.content:
RFC 1646 defines the TN3287 protocol for 3270 printer support. The client identifies itself as an IBM-3287-1 printer using the TERMINAL-TYPE option. To request a specific LU, the client adds a @ symbol followed by the LU name in the terminal type string. For example: IBM-3287-1 @ LUNAME.

Before any print data flows, the client and server must negotiate TERMINAL-TYPE and BINARY mode. The TELNET End-Of-Record (EOR) delimiter separates print data chains and indicates when the client should send status. The maximum Request Unit size is server-specific but should not exceed 4 kilobytes.
sections.eli5: When connecting, the client announces it is printer model 3287 and optionally names which printer to use. Then both sides agree to exchange binary data with EOR (end of record) markers.

sections.title: Print Data Streams and Status Messages
sections.content:
LU 1 and LU 3 print data are distinguished by a prefix byte. LU 1 data is preceded by a zero byte (0x00), which the client must discard. LU 3 data has no prefix and starts directly with the Write-Command-Code (WCC). After the server sends an EOR, the client must respond with a status message showing whether it is ready for more data or has encountered an error.

The status message contains two bytes describing the printer state. Status/Sense Byte 0 Bit 6 is the Device End bit, indicating the printer is ready. Bit 5 signals Unit Specify (error). Status/Sense Byte 1 carries error details: Command Rejected, Intervention Required (not ready), Component Disconnected, Data Check, or Operation Check. The server sends an IAC AO (Abort Output) sequence to signal end-of-bracket (end of print job).
sections.eli5: Printer data comes in with a marker telling you what type it is. After each chunk, the printer reports back: ready, or if something is wrong like paper jam or power off.

sections.title: Error Conditions and Recovery
sections.content:
The RFC defines error conditions that require aborting the connection. The server detects errors and negotiates the client back to NVT (network virtual terminal, plain ASCII) mode by sending WONT/DONT BINARY. The server then sends a numeric error message describing the problem.

Common errors include: no LUs of the requested type configured, the requested LU unavailable, type mismatch between request and configuration, or the LU not configured. The client can shut down if it receives data of an unexpected type (e.g., LU 3 when it only supports LU 1), or continue in the hope of recovery. Temporary conditions like unavailability can be retried.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong (printer not installed, configuration mismatch, not available right now), the server sends an error number. Some errors are temporary and can be retried; others mean configuration needs to change.

sections.title: Security and Future Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC explicitly states that it does not specify how to authenticate that a client is authorized to access a particular LU. This is left to individual server implementations. The RFC notes that the protocol design allows for future incorporation of encryption and authentication RFCs, but some protocol extensions may be needed to integrate them cleanly.

The informational nature of this RFC allowed implementations to be deployed without waiting for standards to fully solidify. However, this also meant that security approaches varied, making it important for administrators to configure access controls at the application level.
sections.eli5: The protocol does not say who is allowed to request which printer. That's up to the server to decide. Security for encryption and passwords can be added later if needed.
